worksheet.title: Find the Loop Bug
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, find, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find the bug in a loop and fix it.

parts.title: Coders fix bugs
text: A bug is a mistake in code. Coders read carefully to FIND the bug, then FIX it — like finding a wrong step in a set of directions.
A loop bug is usually one of two things: the wrong repeat number, or a wrong block inside. Help Bit find and fix them.

parts.title: Bit should JUMP 5 times — but this loop is buggy
parts.note: Bit only jumps 3 times. The repeat number is wrong — it should be 5.

parts.caption: Find the wrong number, then fix it: repeat 3 → repeat 5.

parts.title: Find the bug
parts.prompt: Bit should jump 5 times, but the loop says repeat 3. What is wrong? What should the repeat number be? ______

parts.title: Fix the inside
parts.prompt: Bit should stamp red, blue. But the loop's inside is: stamp red, stamp red. Which block is wrong, and what should it be?

parts.title: Fix the count
parts.prompt: Bit should move 30 steps in total, 10 each time. The loop says repeat 2. What repeat number fixes it? ______

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: This loop is repeat 4 with TWO "move" blocks inside. Bit moved 8 times but should move only 4. Is the bug the repeat number or the inside blocks? Fix it and explain.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To debug a loop, first say what it SHOULD do, then read what it DOES. The bug is usually the repeat number or a block inside — change the one that is wrong.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students read a buggy loop, decide whether the bug is the repeat number or an inside block, and fix it so the code matches the goal. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the blocks and what Bit does, so you can teach from the printout. Optional: a Scratch-style app to drag the blocks and watch Bit run — you only press the green flag.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). Compare the loop to the goal: is the repeat number wrong, or is an inside block wrong?
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Bit should jump 5 times but the loop says repeat 3; fix the repeat number.
3. Let them work. Students fix a wrong inside block (Ex 2), a wrong repeat (Ex 3), and decide which part is the bug (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — the repeat number is wrong; it should be repeat 5. Exercise 2 — the second block is wrong; change "stamp red" to "stamp blue".
Exercise 3 — repeat 3 (3 × 10 = 30 steps). Exercise 4 (challenge) — the inside is the bug: there are two move blocks; remove one so repeat 4 gives 4 moves.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: always blaming the repeat number. Sometimes an inside block is the bug.
Make it easier: ask first "is the count wrong, or is one of the actions wrong?"
Make it harder: ask them to name the bug type for each exercise.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child decides whether the repeat number or an inside block is wrong and fixes it to match the goal.
